solutions.latex:
Method 1:

$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left[\log_e(x+1)-\log_e(x-2)\right]\\&=\dfrac{1}{x+1}-\dfrac{1}{x-2}\end{aligned}$$

OR Method 2: $y=\ln f(x)$, $y'=\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ and quotient rule.

$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}\times\dfrac{(x-2)\times1-(x+1)\times1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{x-2}{x+1}\times\dfrac{x-2-x-1}{(x-2)^2}\\&=\dfrac{-3}{(x+1)(x-2)}\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: Method 1: 1: correct use of log law; 1: correct differentiation of both. Method 2: 1: $\dfrac{1}{\frac{x+1}{x-2}}$; 1: correct quotient rule $\dfrac{-3}{(x-2)^2}$. Marker: this type of question has appeared in many past papers; use Method 1.

solutions.latex:
$y=f(1-x)+2$

$y=f(-(x-1))+2$: horizontal dilation (reflect over $y$-axis), horizontal translation 1 right, vertical translation 2 up.

The order in which these transformations are completed is optional, but the horizontal dilation must happen before the horizontal translation:

Option 1: horizontal dilation, horizontal translation, vertical translation; OR Option 2: vertical translation, horizontal dilation, horizontal translation; OR Option 3: horizontal dilation, vertical translation, horizontal translation.

Completion of the transformations (using Option 1):

(1) Horizontal dilation (reflect over $y$-axis): $P(x,y)=(3,-5)$, $P'(-x,y)=(-3,-5)$

(2) Horizontal translation 1 unit right: $P'(-(x-1),y)=(-2,-5)$

(3) Vertical translation 2 units up: $P'(-(x-1),y+2)=(-2,-3)$

The quick way:

$y=f(1-x)+2$

$P(x,y)\rightarrow P'(1-x,y+2)$

$P(3,-5)\rightarrow P'(1-3,-5+2)=P'(-2,-3)$

(This method does not show understanding but was still awarded.)
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: $(-3,-5)$; 1: $(-2,-5)$; $\frac{1}{2}$: $(-2,-3)$; $\frac{1}{2}$: all 3 transformations done in the correct order (zero if reflection order not demonstrated). Marker: many students did not write the function as $y=kf(a(x+b))+c$; some did not do the horizontal dilation before the horizontal translation; many did not use $P'$ notation for the image.

solutions.latex:
$y=x\times\ln x$

Using the product rule:

let $u=x$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}=1$

let $v=\ln x$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x}$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x\times\dfrac{1}{x}+1\times\ln x$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+\ln x$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct derivative

solutions.latex:
Method 1:

$$\begin{aligned}\int 1+\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int 1\,dx+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\x+\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x+C\\\int\ln x\,dx&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$

Method 2:

From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)=\ln x+1$

$\therefore \ln x=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1$

$$\begin{aligned}\int\ln x\,dx&=\int\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\,dx\\&=x\ln x-x+C\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: some progress, e.g. $\int 1+\ln x\,dx=x\ln x+C$ (or $\int\ln x\,dx=\int\frac{d}{dx}(x\ln x)-1\,dx$); 1: $x\ln x-x+C$. Lose $\frac{1}{2}$ for forgetting $+C$ (once only in Booklet 1).

solutions.latex:
$a=35,\ d=-2,\ S_n=260$ cm

$S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2(35)+(n-1)\cdot(-2)\big)&=260\\n(70-2n+2)&=520\\n(72-2n)&=520\\72n-2n^2&=520\\2n^2-72n+520&=0\\n^2-36n+260&=0\\n&=\dfrac{36\pm\sqrt{36^2-4(1)(260)}}{2}\\&=26\text{ or }10\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}T_n&=a+(n-1)d\\&=35+(26-1)(-2)\\&=35+25(-2)\\&=-15\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$

But $T_n$ represents length and lengths cannot be negative, so $n\ne26$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{x^2+2xy+y^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{14xy+2xy}{16}\qquad(x^2+y^2=14xy)\\&=\dfrac{16xy}{16}\\&=xy\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\qquad\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\right)\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ LHS $=$ RHS, as required.

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\sqrt{xy}\right)\qquad\text{from part (a)}\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\end{aligned}$$

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\qquad\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(x+y)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log16\\&=\log(x+y)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}-\log16^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log(x+y)-\log4\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log x+\dfrac{1}{2}\log y\\&=\log x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\log y^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: using any 2 relevant logarithmic laws; 1: substantial progress towards the solution.

solutions.latex:
Sketch the 2 graphs to give an indication of the area that you have to find out.

\exfigure{1371_q30_s1}

Next, find the points of intersection:

$$\begin{aligned}x^2-3x-3&=x+2\\x^2-4x-5&=0\\(x-5)(x+1)&=0\\x=5\text{ or }x&=-1\end{aligned}$$

$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{5}(\text{top curve}-\text{bottom curve})$

Note that this area is going to be the same anywhere in the plane as this region just represents translation anywhere in the plane. So you don't have to actually take the absolute value (if you wish), as long as one graph is above the other anywhere in the domain, even if some area is below the $x$-axis.

$$\begin{aligned}&\int_{-1}^{5}(x+2)-(x^2-3x-3)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(x+2-x^2+3x+3)\,dx\\&=\int_{-1}^{5}(-x^2+4x+5)\,dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+2x^2+5x\right]_{-1}^{5}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{5^3}{3}+2(5)^2+5(5)\right)-\left(+\dfrac{1}{3}-2+5\right)\\&=36\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: points of intersection $x=5$ or $x=-1$; 1: correct integrand $-x^2+4x+5$; 1: correct primitive; 1: 36 units$^2$. Marker: poorly attempted.
review_reasons: Guidelines' lower-limit line reads $-\left(+\frac{1}{3}-2+5\right)$ (transcribed as written); the correct value is $\frac{1}{3}+2-5$, which gives the stated 36.

$S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$

$a=\sin^2x\cos^2x$

$r=\dfrac{2\sin^2x\cos^4x}{\sin^2x\cos^2x}$

$r=2\cos^2x$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore S&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-\cos^2x-\cos^2x}\\\therefore S&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\quad\text{as required}\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: correct steps to show $S$; $1\frac{1}{2}$: finding the common ratio $r=2\cos^2x$ and using the limiting sum formula correctly and writing $S=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}$; 1: using the limiting sum formula correctly with an incorrect common ratio; $\frac{1}{2}$: the common ratio was correctly found. Marker: answered well overall but some students applied Ext 1 trig identities to finish the proof, e.g. $\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{1-2\cos^2x}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-(2\cos^2x-1)}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-\cos2x}=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{-(\cos^2x-\sin^2x)}$; this was accepted but is not intended in an Advanced paper.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x\div\cos^2x}{(\sin^2x-\cos^2x)\div\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\tan^2x-1}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\csc^2x(\tan^2x-1)}\qquad\text{since }\csc x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\end{aligned}$$

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\csc^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\dfrac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x}{\cos^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$

Alternative method:

$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{1}{\csc^2x(\tan^2x-1)}&=\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}\left(\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}-1\right)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\cos^2x}-\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}}\times\dfrac{\cos^2x\sin^2x}{\cos^2x\sin^2x}\\&=\dfrac{\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^2x-\cos^2x}\end{aligned}$$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: complete solution; 1: progress towards solution ($\frac{1}{2}$ mark each for using $\csc^2x=\dfrac{1}{\sin^2x}$ and $\tan^2x=\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}$); $\frac{1}{2}$: incorrect methods used to prove but at least one trig identity used correctly. solutions.latex:
$t>0$ and $t^2+1>0$ since square values must be positive

$\therefore\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$ since the quotient of two positives is positive

$\therefore 2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge2$

$\therefore v$ is always a positive value and will never equal zero. This means it is never at rest.

OR using the discriminant: if the particle is at rest,

$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}&=0\\2t^2+2+t&=0\\2t^2+t+2&=0\\\Delta&=1^2-4(2)(2)\\&=-15<0\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ No possible solution

$\therefore$ the particle is never at rest

If $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ is stated: 1 mark if $t^2>0$ stated previously; 1.5 marks if $t^2>0$ AND $t>0$ stated; 0 marks if only $t>0$ stated. 0.5 for observing large values of $t$ (e.g. stating $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ hence $\ne-2$; $\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}=0$). Discriminant method: 1 for reaching $2t^2+t+2=0$; 0.5 for the discriminant or quadratic formula; 0.5 for interpretation of the discriminant. Marker: observing $t\to\infty$ alone does not consider earlier values (e.g. $\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\sin t}{t}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{5}$ but $\frac{\sin t}{t}+\frac{1}{5}=0$ at $t\approx4.10462$ and $4.9063$); practise supporting arguments in explain questions.
